analysis.one_liner: Sends families $667 a month per child aged 2 to 5 enrolled in preschool.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the House with no cosponsors and has sat in the Ways and Means Committee, with no hearing or vote, since its referral on December 11, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a new refundable tax credit of $667 per month ($8,000 a year, adjusted for inflation) for each child aged 2 to 5 whom the family is caring for and who is enrolled in an early childhood education program, including licensed private pre-K. The full amount goes to families below 300% of the poverty line and phases out above that. Families can receive the money monthly during the year instead of waiting for tax season, through an IRS advance-payment system with annual renewal.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children aged 2 to 5 who are enrolled in an early childhood education program and earn below roughly 300% of the poverty line. The credit is fully refundable, so families who owe little or no income tax still receive the full payment, and monthly advance payments put cash in hand when preschool costs come due rather than once a year at tax time.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families with preschool-age children in care

how_it_helps.text: Provides $667 per month per eligible child aged 2 to 5, which comes to $8,004 per child per year before inflation adjustments.
Phases the payment down only above 300% of the poverty line for the family's size, so low- and middle-income families get the full amount.
Makes the credit fully refundable, so families with little or no income tax liability still receive the money.

Lets families get the money as monthly advance payments during the year, with an online portal, automatic enrollment rules tied to government programs, and grace-period and hardship protections against losing payments.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through an increase in the deficit. The bill text contains no tax increases or spending cuts to offset the new credit.

drawbacks.text: The bill has no pay-for: it adds a new multi-billion-dollar annual entitlement to the deficit with no revenue offset anywhere in the text.
The credit is conditioned on the child being enrolled in an early childhood education program, so a family caring for a 3-year-old at home, or using informal or unlicensed care, gets nothing.
The credit covers only ages 2 to 5; infants and school-age children are excluded.

Monthly advance payments based on a prior year's income can overshoot what a family ultimately qualifies for, and the bill requires the family to repay the excess, with tax increases for changes in income, ineligibility, or claimed fraud.
The program is administratively complex: annual renewals, competing-claim adjudication between separated parents, and detailed care-determination rules all fall on the IRS to build.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For eligible families the benefit is large and immediate, comparable to the expanded 2021 child tax credit but targeted at preschool-age children in care. The honest cost is fiscal: nothing in the bill pays for it, so it is a deficit-financed transfer. The enrollment requirement also means some equally needy stay-at-home families are left out. As written it is a straightforward, if expensive, family benefit, not a program with hidden costs to the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill is brand new: it was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it awaits a hearing or markup that has not been scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Cleo Fields introduced the bill in the House on December 11, 2025.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which has jurisdiction over tax legislation; no further action has been taken.
No other member has cosponsored the bill.

The bill would create a refundable credit of $667 per month per child aged 2 to 5 enrolled in an early childhood education program, phased out above 300% of the poverty line, with monthly advance payments and inflation indexing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet, because the bill has only been referred to committee and nothing has been decided.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; bill awaits committee action

for.name: Rep. Cleo Fields
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House and it was referred to Ways and Means.

sides.party_line_note: No cosponsors have joined from either party and no vote has occurred, so no partisan split is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Private pre-K and early childhood education providers
industries.note: The credit is only payable for a child enrolled in a licensed or state-regulated early childhood education program, explicitly including private pre-K, so the new federal money partly flows to these programs and makes enrollment the permanent gateway to the benefit. Their interest runs alongside families', since both gain from the subsidy.

analysis.trajectory: A first-term member's tax bill with zero cosponsors, referred to Ways and Means in mid-December, faces long odds. Unless it attracts cosponsors and a committee hearing, the likely path is to sit in committee and expire when this Congress ends in January 2027, like the large majority of introduced bills.
